language_wrapper: The Bank of Pittsburgh issues coins that have a heads side and a tails side. Vera has a row of {n} such coins alternately tails-up and heads-up, with the leftmost coin tails-up. On a move, Vera may flip over one coin, subject to the rules: (i) on the first move, Vera may flip any of the {n} coins; (ii) on all subsequent moves, Vera may only flip over a coin adjacent to the coin she flipped on the previous move. Additionally, flipping the i-th coin incurs a cost c_i, and the costs are given in order from left to right as: [costs_str]. Determine the smallest possible total cost Vera can incur to reach a state in which every coin is heads-up.
teacher_generator_code:
def generator(rng):
    # Choose n moderately large to avoid trivial cases but keep the verifier simple
    n = rng.randint(5, 60)  # ensure at least one interior coin
    # Generate diverse positive integer costs
    costs = [rng.randint(1, 50) for _ in range(n)]
    # Ensure not all costs are equal (to avoid trivial uniform-cost instances)
    if len(set(costs)) == 1:
        # retry once; if still uniform, tweak one entry
        costs = [rng.randint(1, 50) for _ in range(n)]
        if len(set(costs)) == 1:
            idx = rng.randint(0, n-1)
            costs[idx] = costs[idx] + 1
    costs_str = " ".join(str(x) for x in costs)
    return {'n': n, 'costs_str': costs_str, 'costs': costs}
hardness_rationale: The family upgrades the original adjacency-flip problem by introducing heterogeneous flipping costs per position and asking for the minimal total cost, not merely the minimal number of moves. Solving requires proving structural optimality of flip counts under adjacency constraints (endpoints once, interiors twice, with the right endpoint flipped only when n is odd), essentially an exchange or invariant argument about necessary parity and traversal. The seed’s simple count 2n−2 generalizes to cost-weighted optimization with case distinctions by parity of n, and participants must justify that no cheaper scheme can reduce the number of flips of interior positions below two while meeting the parity requirement. This heightened combinatorial and parity reasoning goes beyond the seed and cannot be solved by guessing.
notes:
Proof sketch of correctness: Label the coins 1..n left to right. The initial state is alternating with coin 1 tails; hence coin i is tails iff i is odd. In any valid sequence of flips, coin i is flipped exactly the number of times it is visited by the walk (the sequence of flipped indices), since each visit flips the coin. The goal is to flip each odd-position coin an odd number of times and each even-position coin an even number of times. Consider any walk respecting adjacency that meets the goal. For 2 <= i <= n-1 (interior coins), the walk must enter and later leave the interval to reach tails on both sides; a standard parity/invariant argument shows that every interior coin must be flipped at least twice. More formally, focusing on the edges (i−1,i) and (i,i+1), any walk that changes the parity of both adjacent odd-position tails necessarily traverses both edges around i in a way that forces two visits (flips) to i, and any attempt to reduce flips at i violates the even-parity requirement at an even index or the odd-parity requirement at a neighboring odd index. For endpoints: coin 1 starts as tails and must be flipped at least once; coin n is tails iff n is odd (so it needs at least one flip only in that case). The constructive upper bound is achieved by a zig-zag walk: for odd n, flip sequence 1,2,1,2,3,2,3,4,...,n−1,n,n−1; for even n, 1,2,1,2,3,2,3,4,...,n−2,n−1,n−2. In both cases, each interior coin is flipped exactly twice, coin 1 exactly once, and coin n exactly once iff it is initially tails (n odd). Thus the minimal total cost equals c_1 + 2*sum_{i=2}^{n−1} c_i + [c_n if n is odd else 0]. Any deviation that reduces flips on any interior coin below two would force parity failure or add flips elsewhere that increase or equal total cost; hence this pattern is optimal.
Implementation note: The verifier reconstructs the costs from the provided string and applies the closed-form formula, validating input consistency and guarding against trivial instances. The generator ensures randomized, diverse costs and sufficiently large n to prevent trivialities.
source_question:
The Bank of Pittsburgh issues coins that have a heads side and a tails side. Vera
has a row of 7873 such coins alternately tails-up and heads-up, with the leftmost
coin tails-up.
In a move, Vera may flip over one of the coins in the row, subject to the following
rules:
• On the first move, Vera may flip over any of the 7873 coins.
• On all subsequent moves, Vera may only flip over a coin adjacent to the coin
she flipped on the previous move. (We do not consider a coin to be adjacent
to itself.)
Determine the smallest possible number of moves Vera can make to reach a state in
which every coin is heads-up.
